title: Why Use Stochastic?
description: Compute [probability distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_probability_distributions) directly in DuckDB SQL — [PDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function), [CDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function), [quantile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantile_function), [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_rate), and random sampling for 22 named distributions, all with a uniform `dist_<family>_<op>` naming scheme. Built for Monte Carlo experiments, what-if analysis, and synthetic data generation without leaving SQL.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: Stochastic gives DuckDB a complete statistical-distributions library. Each of 22 distributions exposes the same uniform set of operations, so once you've used one you've used them all. Best fit: ad-hoc analysis, Monte Carlo sketches, [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data) generation, hypothesis-test p-values, and inline statistical math in SQL pipelines.

bulletPoints.label: Monte Carlo and what-if analysis
bulletPoints.description: Run a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) by combining `_sample` functions with [`range()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/nested.html). Aggregate the draws with regular SQL — no Python, no DataFrame round-trip.

bulletPoints.label: Synthetic data generation
bulletPoints.description: Populate test fixtures or anonymized columns with realistic distributions in a single [`CREATE TABLE AS`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table). Mix-and-match heights from [`dist_normal_sample`](#dist_normal_sample), counts from [`dist_poisson_sample`](#dist_poisson_sample), wait times from [`dist_exponential_sample`](#dist_exponential_sample).

bulletPoints.label: Inline statistical math
bulletPoints.description: Compute [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score), p-values, [Value at Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_at_risk), or Bayesian credible intervals as plain SQL expressions. [`dist_normal_cdf_complement`](#dist_normal_cdf_complement) for tail probabilities, [`dist_chi_squared_cdf`](#dist_chi_squared_cdf) for goodness-of-fit, [`dist_beta_quantile`](#dist_beta_quantile) for posterior intervals.

bulletPoints.label: Distribution properties as functions
bulletPoints.description: Mean, median, mode, variance, skewness, kurtosis, support range — every property is a function (not a constant), so it composes inline anywhere a value is allowed.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension wraps the [Boost.Math statistical-distributions library](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/release/libs/math/doc/html/dist.html) — the same battle-tested implementations used across C++ statistics tooling. Every distribution gets the same 21-operation surface, generated from a single template; that's where the ~444 function count comes from.

bulletPoints.label: Uniform naming: `dist_<family>_<op>`
bulletPoints.description: Every function is named `dist_<distribution>_<operation>`. The operation suffix is one of `sample`, `pdf`, `log_pdf`, `cdf`, `log_cdf`, `cdf_complement`, `log_cdf_complement`, `quantile`, `quantile_complement`, `hazard`, `chf`, `mean`, `median`, `mode`, `variance`, `stddev`, `skewness`, `kurtosis`, `kurtosis_excess`, `range`, `support`.

bulletPoints.label: Parameter-then-x argument order
bulletPoints.description: Distribution parameters come first; the evaluation point comes last. `dist_normal_pdf(mean, stddev, x)`, `dist_binomial_cdf(n, p, k)`. Property functions ([`dist_normal_mean`](#dist_normal_mean), etc.) take only the distribution parameters.

bulletPoints.label: Vectorized over columns
bulletPoints.description: All functions are scalar — they run column-at-a-time over DuckDB's columnar engine, so a million calls in a `SELECT` over `range(1000000)` is a single vectorized scan, not a Python loop.

bulletPoints.label: Strict parameter validation
bulletPoints.description: Illegal parameters raise a SQL error — no silent NaN. `dist_normal_pdf(0, -1, 0.5)` returns `Error: normal: Standard deviation must be > 0`. This catches typos in long pipelines that NumPy would otherwise carry forward as silent NaNs.

bulletPoints.label: Log-scale variants
bulletPoints.description: Every PDF/CDF has [`_log_pdf`](#dist_normal_log_pdf) / [`_log_cdf`](#dist_normal_log_cdf) / [`_log_cdf_complement`](#dist_normal_log_cdf_complement) variants for log-likelihoods and very-small-tail probabilities — direct computation in log space avoids underflow.

sections.title: Scope and honest caveats
sections.description: This extension is a deep statistical-distributions library, but it is intentionally not a full simulation framework. Know the boundaries before you reach for it.

bulletPoints.label: No copulas or multivariate distributions
bulletPoints.description: The 22 distributions are univariate. There is no [copula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)) or multivariate-normal sampler in this version — for correlated draws, sample independently and apply a [Cholesky-style transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholesky_decomposition) yourself, or use NumPy / SciPy.

bulletPoints.label: RNG seeding is not user-controlled
bulletPoints.description: `_sample` functions use the underlying [PRNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_number_generator) — there is no documented per-query seed parameter. For exactly-reproducible runs (papers, regulatory submissions), generate the draws once into a table and treat that table as the seed.

bulletPoints.label: Production simulation may want a notebook
bulletPoints.description: For large-scale agent-based simulation, MCMC, or anything needing [SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html)-grade fitting, keep a Python notebook with NumPy / SciPy. Stochastic shines for quick analyses, what-if exploration, and synthetic-data generation that lives next to your warehouse data.

bulletPoints.label: No fitting / inference helpers
bulletPoints.description: The extension is one-way: parameters → distribution. There are no MLE / method-of-moments fitters and no built-in hypothesis tests; compute the test statistic in SQL, then call the appropriate `_cdf_complement` for the p-value.

useCases.title: Monte Carlo over warehouse data
useCases.description: Wrap [`dist_normal_sample`](#dist_normal_sample) / [`dist_uniform_real_sample`](#dist_uniform_real_sample) in a CTE over `range(N)` and aggregate with SQL — estimate π, integrate a payoff function, run a [VaR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_at_risk) calculation against live position data, all without leaving the warehouse.

useCases.title: Generate realistic synthetic data
useCases.description: Build a fixture table with [`CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table): heights from a [Normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution), session counts from a [Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution), session lengths from an [Exponential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution), conversion flags from a [Bernoulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_distribution). One query, hundreds of thousands of rows.

useCases.title: Inline p-values and confidence intervals
useCases.description: Compute a Z-statistic, then `2 * dist_normal_cdf_complement(0, 1, ABS(z))` for the two-sided p-value. Same shape works for [`dist_chi_squared_cdf_complement`](#dist_chi_squared_cdf_complement) and [`dist_students_t_cdf_complement`](#dist_students_t_cdf_complement) — analytics dashboards with first-class statistics.

useCases.title: Bayesian conjugate updates
useCases.description: [Beta-Binomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior#Discrete_distributions), Gamma-Poisson, Normal-Normal — closed-form posteriors are one [`dist_<family>_quantile`](#dist_beta_quantile) call away. Useful for A/B-test dashboards and conversion-rate experiments.
